s470: ScamSense protects you from scams. It checks your email (Gmail, every folder), text messages, phone numbers, and crypto websites, and tells you in plain words what's safe and what to do. It also has Pause before you pay, a step-by-step plan if you were scammed, short lessons, and a Family tab for people you trust. I'm Mahi, its helper. Your messages are checked on your device and never sold.
s471: I'm Mahi, an AI helper, so I'm not a live person. To talk to a real person about a scam: call a family member or friend you trust (see the Family tab), the AARP Fraud Watch Network Helpline at 877-908-3360 (free, Mon–Fri), or, if you're 60 or older, the National Elder Fraud Hotline at 1-833-372-8311. If you already lost money, call your bank now using the number on your card.
s472: I'm sorry this happened. It's not your fault. Act fast: call your bank or card company now using the number on the back of your card, stop all contact with the scammer, and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Tap below and ScamSense will build your full recovery plan and documents.
s473: Paying with gift cards is always a scam. No real company, bank, or government office takes gift cards as payment. Don't buy them and don't read the numbers to anyone. If you already gave the numbers, call the number on the back of the card right away.
s474: Texts about unpaid tolls or missed packages are almost always fake. Don't tap the link. Check your account by typing the official website yourself, or open the official app. You can forward the text to 7726 to report it, then delete it.
s475: Government offices like the IRS, Social Security, and Medicare never call to demand money, threaten arrest, or ask for gift cards or crypto. Hang up. If you're worried, call the office yourself using the number on its official website.
s476: Your bank will never ask you to move money to a "safe account" or to send a Zelle payment to protect yourself. Hang up and call the number on the back of your card. Caller ID can be faked, so a call that shows your bank's name can still be a scam.
s477: Never share a code that was texted to you, not even with someone who says they're your bank. That code lets them into your account. If you already shared it, change your password now and call the company.
s478: This sounds like the "grandparent scam." Before you do anything, call your family member at the number you already have, or call their parents. Real emergencies can wait a few minutes. Don't send money, gift cards, or cash with a courier.
s479: Real tech companies don't call you or show pop-ups with a phone number. Close the window and don't call. Never let a stranger control your computer, and never pay a "refund" back. If you already gave access, disconnect from the internet and get help from someone you trust.
s480: You can't win a contest you never entered, and a real prize never makes you pay first. If they ask for a fee, taxes, or your bank details to get your prize, it's a scam.
s481: Be very careful. Guaranteed or daily profits, a stranger who moves the chat to WhatsApp or Telegram, or a fee to withdraw your own money are signs of a crypto scam. Crypto can't be reversed. Paste the website or wallet address here and I'll check it, or open the crypto check.
